questions.prompt: What is `never`, and where is it most useful?

options.text: The type of any value; useful for logging
The bottom type with no values; most useful for exhaustiveness checks that force handling every union member
A synonym for undefined
The type of empty arrays

questions.explanation: never has no values. Assigning a switch's default case to a never variable makes the compiler error if a new union member isn't handled.

questions.prompt: Does a type assertion (`as`) perform a runtime check or conversion?

options.text: Yes, it validates the value at runtime
No — it's a compile-time-only override; if you're wrong, the bug surfaces at runtime
It converts the value to the target type
It throws if the types don't match

questions.explanation: An assertion only tells the compiler to treat a value as a type. It emits no runtime check or conversion, so an incorrect assertion causes runtime bugs.

questions.prompt: What does `satisfies` do that a type annotation does not?

options.text: It converts the value at runtime
It validates a value against a type without widening the value's inferred type, preserving precise literal/member types
It disables type checking for the value
It makes the value readonly

questions.explanation: satisfies checks that a value conforms to a type while keeping its specific inferred types — unlike an annotation, which widens the value to the target type.

questions.prompt: When should you avoid the non-null assertion `!`?

options.text: Never — it's always safe
Whenever a real check or default is possible — a wrong `!` crashes at runtime
Only inside classes
Only when the value is a number

questions.explanation: The ! operator claims a value isn't null/undefined with no runtime check. Prefer a real check or default; a wrong assertion crashes at runtime.

questions.prompt: To force a cast between unrelated types you must route through `as unknown as Type`, which bypasses TypeScript's ______ rule. (one word)
questions.explanation: TypeScript allows assertions only between sufficiently overlapping types; going through unknown bypasses that overlap rule — a red flag.

questions.prompt: Why prefer `unknown` over `any` for a `catch` clause or parsed JSON?

options.text: It is faster
It forces you to narrow before using the value, preventing silent runtime errors
It validates the value automatically
any is not allowed in catch

questions.explanation: unknown requires narrowing before use, so you must check the value's actual shape — catching mistakes that any would let slip through silently.
